title: Closing the Approximation Gap in Simulation-free Latent SDEs
claim: Prior methods fix one drift per set of marginals and miss the true posterior; adding a marginal-preserving correction closes the gap.
layout: 3 regions left-to-right; dashed box in middle with vector-field panels linked by arrows
description: The figure has three parts, A, B and C, read left to right. Panel A is a time-series sketch of a latent state x1 between times 4 and 5. A purple true-posterior curve with a shaded band sits above a red reference-drift curve with its band. Each curve ends at a different point on a marginal density drawn at the right edge, and a legend names the two curves. A red arrow runs from A into the dashed rounded box, which is panel B. Inside B are three square vector-field plots linked by thick black arrows. The first shows the reference posterior drift f_q as parallel arrows. The second shows the residual field r = f_p - f_q as a rotational swirl over a purple blob. The third shows the corrected drift. A blue arrow leads from the third plot to panel C. Panel C repeats A's axes with a blue Helmholtz-SDE curve that matches the purple posterior. Red, purple and blue colour-code the three drifts or posteriors.
caption: Overview of Helmholtz-SDE. A: Existing simulation-free VI algorithms commit to a single drift (red) for each set of one-time marginals (black). This choice induces transition distributions that can differ from those of the true posterior (purple), even when the one-time marginals agree. B: Helmholtz-SDE takes a drift consistent with a set of one-time marginals, then corrects it by a vector field that preserves the marginals. C: The resulting approximation (blue) better matches the posterior.
abstract: Recovering dynamical systems from noisy observations is a recurring challenge across scientific domains, including neuroscience and physics. Latent stochastic differential equations (SDEs) address this by modeling the system as an unobserved state that evolves according to a learnable SDE and generates the observations. Variational inference (VI) provides a tractable objective for fitting latent SDEs. Traditional VI algorithms evaluate this objective by numerical simulation over a time discretization, trading fidelity for computational cost. A recent class of algorithms, simulation-free VI, sidesteps this tradeoff by parameterizing the posterior through its instantaneous marginals rather than its drift. In this work, we show that the efficiency of existing simulation-free VI algorithms comes at a price: their parameterizations restrict the approximate posterior to a subset of the SDEs available to simulation-based methods, degrading posterior inference and parameter learning. We propose Helmholtz-SDE, a simulation-free VI algorithm that closes this gap by optimizing over path laws compatible with a prescribed collection of marginals. Helmholtz-SDE recovers dynamics more faithfully than prior simulation-free methods, with the largest gains under high posterior uncertainty. It further matches the performance of simulation-based VI at a fraction of the runtime. Code is available at https://github.com/lindermanlab/helmholtz-sde .
